transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-06-02 11:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sam (Redwood SE), Eli (Redwood), Alex (OmniIndex Head of ML), Priya (CTO), Morgan (Staff Eng), Tomasz (Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on whether OmniIndex should use Redwood hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) for a high-throughput reranking pipeline. Major concerns: tail latency under load, embedding dimensionality tradeoffs, vector DB integration (fanout vs local rerank), encryption/KMS, and cost projection. Agreed next steps and action items.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and pain points
- Throughput targets and latency SLOs
- Vector DB topology and rerank placement
- Embedding dimension vs retrieval quality tradeoffs
- Hosting security controls (VPC, KMS, audit logs)
- Pilot scope and success metrics

Notes/Links:
- Shared deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/omniindex-rerank-05-2028 (placeholder)
- Benchmark template: drive.google.com/benchmark-omniindex (placeholder)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros and then jump into what you folks are trying to solve with rerank.
[00:10] Alex: Hi yeah I'm Alex, head of ML at OmniIndex. We're building a unified search layer that merges user signals + product catalog, we have a vector DB for initial recall and then a neural reranker.
[00:18] Priya: Priya here, CTO. We're evaluating whether to offload inference to Redwood-hosted or keep dedicated on AWS for compliance reasons.
[00:25] Sam: Great — I'm Sam SE, I focus on embeddings and throughput. Before we dive, what's your current QPS and SLOs?
[00:32] Morgan: Currently we see avg 800 qps during peak, spikes to ~3k qps for short windows. SLO is 95th percentile end-to-end search latency under 350ms.
[00:43] Jordan: Ok, good. And the retriever + rerank breakdown today?
[00:48] Alex: Retriever is ~40-60ms, that's our vector DB (self-hosted Milvus right now), then we fanout top-100 to a reranker model (we use a fine-tuned cross-encoder) which is the heavy bit. Reranker p95 is around 210ms when not overloaded, but tails are bad.
[01:05] Sam: When you say fanout to top-100 — are you running rerank on the application side against embeddings or using the model to re-embed/rerank on the server?
[01:12] Alex: We pull the top-100 doc IDs then fetch content and do the cross-encoder on our side. So the latency is a combo of fetch time + model inference.
[01:20] Priya: Also worth noting we have strict data residency for EU customers, and we need audit logs and KMS integration.
[01:27] Jordan: Understood. So big decision levers: where rerank executes (Redwood-hosted, Redwood-dedicated, or private VPC), and whether to quantize/compact embeddings to reduce cost.
[01:36] Morgan: Quick question on dimensionality — our embeddings are 1536 dims right now from a proprietary embedder. We've seen drop in recall with 512 dims in some tests. Wondering best practice for hybrid search + rerank.
[01:47] Sam: Yeah this is common. A typical pattern is keep higher-dim embeddings for dense recall and use an initial cheap vector index on smaller dims for candidate recall, then rely on reranker to do final scoring. But tradeoff if you reduce dims you save storage/IO and initial fanout costs but may increase rerank load.
[02:03] Alex: So would Redwood recommend running rerank co-located with the vector DB, or keep it centrally in a low-latency region?
[02:10] Eli: From the runtime side, colocating rerank with the index can cut fetch latencies but complicates scaling since the model infra has different scaling profile than the index. Redwood routing can route requests to nearby model pools or fallback to cheaper quantized variants if capacity is constrained.
[02:28] Jordan: I'd add that one hybrid approach we've seen is: run initial recall in regional edge index, then do rerank in a centralized dedicated pool that has autoscale and batching optimized. That typically gives consistent p95s at cost that is economical.
[02:41] Priya: Autoscale — how fast can dedicated pools scale for sudden spikes?
[02:45] Sam: We support configurable autoscale policies. For dedicated capacity you can reserve baseline and allow burst; spin-up times depend on backend but typical warm-up for extra GPUs is a few minutes. For immediate spikes we recommend a small burst buffer or multi-tier fallback to hosted.
[02:59] Morgan: What about latency variability introduced by batching? If you use bigger batches to reduce cost per token, do we risk missing SLOs?
[03:07] Sam: Correct, batching improves throughput but increases tail latency. Redwood Optimize will suggest batch sizes for your latency targets and workloads; you can set per-route latency SLOs and the runtime will keep batching within that constraint, plus continuous batching helps hide small inefficiencies.
[03:21] Alex: Can you talk about KV cache and prefix caching? We do a lot of near-duplicate queries.
[03:26] Sam: We have automatic prefix/KV caching so repeated prefixes or rerank inputs can use cached KV states when safe — it reduces tokens and inference cost for repeated contexts. But for rerank with different candidates caching is limited.
[03:37] Tomasz: On the vector DB side, our Milvus cluster is sharded across AZs. We worry about egress and cross-AZ fetch costs if we colocate rerank elsewhere. Any advice?
[03:47] Eli: If you colocate, you can place model pools in the same AZs to avoid cross-AZ egress. For hosted options, Redwood can route to region-specific pools to minimize egress, and for Private we can be deployed in your VPC to avoid cloud egress charges.
[03:59] Priya: Security — SSO, RBAC, audit logs, HSM/KMS. Do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:06] Jordan: Yes, for Private and Dedicated we support KMS/HSM integrations and full audit logs. Hosted has envelope encryption and SOC2 controls, but if you need customer-managed KMS, Private is typical.
[04:16] Alex: Competitors like Pinecone say they can do managed indexes with lower management friction — what's Redwood's advantage?
[04:23] Jordan: Our differentiation is a production-first runtime optimized for LLM inference with batching, KV cache, automatic quantization recommendations, and unified tooling across hosted/dedicated/private. We also provide the rerank-first patterns (routing, fallback variants) to keep apps online under load.
[04:36] Morgan: Let's discuss an example flow at scale — say 3k qps spike, each query fans out to top-100, then rerank. What are options to reduce cost?
[04:45] Sam: Options: reduce fanout (top-20), use a two-stage rerank (cheap lightweight scorer then heavy cross-encoder on top-k), quantize the rerank model to int8/4 if quality allows, or move rerank to dedicated hardware with higher throughput. You can also cache rerank results for repeated queries.
[05:02] Alex: Any numbers on cost delta for those strategies?
[05:05] Jordan: Rough ballparks — moving from top-100 to top-20 reduces rerank compute by ~5x. Quantizing model to int8 might reduce GPU hours by 30-40%. Dedicated pools can give 20-60% better unit economics depending on commit level. We'll share a TCO spreadsheet with specific numbers for your load.
[05:23] Tomasz: About embeddings: we have 1536 dims at the moment. If we wanted to try sparse or compact embeddings, does Redwood have tooling to evaluate quality-vs-econ?
[05:33] Sam: Redwood Optimize has eval harnesses — you can run quality regressions across prompt sets and embedding variants. We can help run a dimension sweep (1536 -> 1024 -> 512) and measure recall + rerank lift.
[05:44] Priya: For the pilot, what would success criteria look like?
[05:47] Jordan: We recommend: p95 end-to-end under 350ms at baseline load, rerank quality within 1-2% of current metric (NDCG@10), and clear cost-per-query projection showing savings or acceptable delta. Also security checklist pass (KMS, SSO, audit).
[06:02] Alex: Timeline — we want a 2-week smoke test then a 6-8 week pilot. Is that feasible?
[06:07] Sam: Yes, for smoke test we can provision a test model and run throughput tests with your sample vectors. Pilot would be Dedicated or Private depending on your security needs.
[06:15] Morgan: A technical nit — concurrency: if we have many concurrent rerank requests with varying sequence lengths, how does Redwood handle KV cache invalidation?
[06:24] Eli: Kernel and KV cache management is per model/context; the runtime manages KV TTLs and garbage collection. For rerank where inputs are shorter and mostly fixed-length, KV is less of a factor than for chat.
[06:35] Jordan: Also, for variable seqs we recommend batching windows tuned to your latency SLOs so you don't significantly increase variance.
[06:41] Alex: Any gotchas around model compatibility? Our reranker is a custom fine-tuned model in PyTorch.
[06:47] Sam: We support common model formats; if you have custom ops we can work through conversion or run as a container in Dedicated/Private. We'll do a quick compatibility check during the smoke test.
[06:58] Priya: On SLA and outages — if you host with Redwood, what's the fallback if a region degrades?
[07:05] Jordan: Routing has automatic fallbacks to compatible model variants and other regions; you can also configure multi-region pools or fail to a cheaper hosted tier. There's a tradeoff with latency but keeps service available.
[07:15] Tomasz: Ok let's talk about integration work — what do you need from us to run the smoke test?
[07:21] Sam: A small dataset: 10k-100k vectors, 1k-5k sample queries, and a brief spec of current fanout pattern and infra. Also credentials or test access to a non-prod vector index if you want end-to-end.
[07:33] Tomasz: We can export vector snapshots, might be heavy but doable. We'll prepare a 25k vector sample and 2k queries.
[07:39] Jordan: Great. We'll also provide a load script and a benchmark sheet template.
[07:45] Alex: On cost, Priya asks: if we do dedicated reserved capacity, what's the minimum commit?
[07:51] Jordan: We have small reserve tiers; practical minimum for meaningful TCO is usually a month commit of 1-2 GPU-equivalent nodes. We'll include exact numbers in the pricing doc.
[07:59] Morgan: Would Redwood run the rerank model in CPU fallback if GPUs aren't available?
[08:04] Eli: CPU fallback is possible but will severely increase latency and is not recommended for production rerank workloads. Better to have a multi-tier fallback policy with smaller models or quantized variants.
[08:15] Alex: How do we measure rerank lift for the pilot? We use NDCG and CTR.
[08:20] Sam: We'll help instrument evaluation harness and can run A/B experiments using the rollout features — canary and automatic fallback if quality regressions occur.
[08:29] Priya: Cost of data egress if we keep vector DB in our VPC and use hosted Redwood?
[08:34] Jordan: Egress costs depend on your cloud provider. For high fanout it's often cheaper to colocate model pools or go Dedicated/Private. We'll estimate egress in the TCO spreadsheet.
[08:44] Tomasz: About logs — we need per-request trace and token-level cost.
[08:49] Jordan: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and per-route latencies, trace IDs, and exportable logs for audits. For Private, logs stay inside your VPC.
[08:58] Alex: If we decide Private deployment, how long to get running?
[09:02] Sam: Private VPC deployment onboarding is typically 4-8 weeks depending on network approvals and security posture. Dedicated is faster, hosted fastest for first smoke tests.
[09:12] Priya: Ok that aligns with our timeline.
[09:14] Jordan: Quick recap then next steps.
[09:17] Jordan: Action items — Sam will provision smoke test infra and run throughput simulation, Tomasz will provide vector samples, Jordan will send TCO/pricing and security checklist. We'll aim to reconvene after smoke test results.
[09:29] Alex: Sounds good; thanks everyone.
[09:31] Priya: Thanks, bye.

End of call.
